lessonTitle: Low-rank joint compression: cache one latent, rebuild every head
md: MLA is not a compression applied to an already trained model's cache, like PCA (principal component analysis, which finds the few directions that capture most of the variation in a set of vectors) run on stored keys. The down- and up-projections are ordinary weights learned from scratch during pretraining. Converting an existing MHA or GQA model to MLA needs extra fine-tuning work (see lesson 7).

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Unmerged does not mean easy. Requests in one batch use adapters with different ranks and different sequence lengths, so padding everything into one batched matmul wastes work. S-LoRA's variant that copies adapters into contiguous memory and uses padded batched matmul (S-LoRA-bmm) was much slower than the version with custom kernels, GPU functions written for exactly this mixed-rank job.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
md: RRF rewards agreement between phrasings. A relevant document that only one phrasing finds stays low, and a junk document that two phrasings share can outrank it. That is why the quality of the phrasings matters as much as their number.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Common misconception: an MTP model does not have to emit several tokens per step. Gloeckle et al. use only the next-token head for ordinary decoding. The other heads are optional, and lesson 7 shows how they can be reused to draft tokens for faster decoding.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
md: Pick the ruler, get the optimizer. Frobenius gives gradient descent, the largest-entry norm gives sign descent (Adam without moving averages), the spectral norm gives the orthogonalized update. For a hidden linear layer the spectral norm is the one that bounds how much its outputs move.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
md: Do not judge an optimizer by a single untuned comparison. The Muon post argues that the most common reason optimizers that claimed to beat AdamW never caught on is an undertuned AdamW baseline, and proposes competitive benchmarks (like the NanoGPT speedrun record, where anyone can revert to AdamW) as the standard of evidence.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: The muP rules, layer by layer
md: Every piece is needed. Keeping $1/\sqrt{d}$ attention, using plain `torch.optim.Adam` instead of `MuAdam`, or forgetting to scale `d_ffn` along with `d_model` silently breaks transfer while the model still trains. Lesson 7 shows how to catch this.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: A lock is two things at once: mutual exclusion (one atomic read-modify-write decides a single winner) and visibility (Acquire on lock, Release on unlock, so each unlock happens-before the next lock).

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC is not the same as no locking. Two transactions that update the *same* row still conflict: the second one waits for the first to commit or roll back. MVCC only stops readers and writers from blocking each other.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
md: SSI = snapshot isolation plus non-blocking tracking of rw edges. It aborts a transaction in any dangerous structure, so every committed set is serializable; the application's job is to retry on 40001.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Why long context needs sparsity, and why bolt-on sparsity disappoints
md: Theoretical FLOP savings are not speedups. A sparse attention method is only fast if the GPU reads fewer bytes in contiguous chunks during every phase (training, prefill, decode), and it only keeps quality if the model is trained with the sparsity.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: pHash: hashing the low frequencies of a DCT
md: aHash compares pixels with the mean, dHash compares neighbors, pHash compares low-frequency DCT coefficients with their median. All three are **global**: they describe the whole frame at fixed positions, which is why resizing and tone changes are cheap to survive and crops, flips and rotations are not.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Where the attacker stands: on-path, off-path and on your LAN
md: Know the position before you pick the defence. Encryption (TLS) defeats on-path reading and rewriting of content. Unpredictable numbers (random ports, sequence numbers, IDs) defeat off-path guessing. Switch features such as MAC limiting, DHCP snooping and ARP inspection stop local attackers from becoming on-path.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Flooding DNS and HTTP/2: Dyn 2016 and Rapid Reset 2023
md: Application-layer floods win through asymmetry: a cheap action for the client (open and cancel a stream) that is expensive for the server. Defences measure behaviour per connection and close abusive connections outright, because per-request blocking leaves the cheap channel open. The pattern recurs: MadeYouReset (CVE-2025-8671, 2025) uses malformed control frames to make the server reset streams itself.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Zeek's protocol logs and pivoting with uid, fuid and Community ID
md: Two IDs carry most investigations: Zeek's uid joins logs about one connection, fuid joins logs about one file. Community ID extends the join to other tools. Learn to move between them quickly; it is most of the job.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation
md: Capture and analyse only traffic you own or are authorised to monitor. Practice pcaps of real infections contain working malware and sometimes real personal data from the lab: open them on an isolated, non-Windows machine and never run extracted files.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ports, sockets and NAT
md: NAT is not a firewall. It drops unsolicited inbound packets only as a side effect of having no table entry. Port-forwarding rules, devices that open forwards automatically, IPv6 (often no NAT at all) and connections started from inside all bypass that "protection". Use an actual firewall policy.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: malloc chooses addresses, the first write chooses the node. Initialize data in parallel with the same pinned threads and the same partitioning that will later use it.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
md: Lifetime and throughput both scale with 1/A. The levers to lower A are all about making victim blocks emptier: more spare, TRIM of dead data, writes that are large and sequential, and grouping data that will die at the same time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Training and tuning a detector in practice
md: The AP number picks the model; the confidence threshold, chosen on validation data that looks like deployment, decides how it behaves.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
md: The shape of the data decides which questions you can ask. Metrics answer "how often, how slow, for everyone". Traces answer "where did the time go inside this one request". Logs answer "what exactly happened at this instant".

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: A dashboard is an ordered list of questions, not a list of metrics. Start with the SLO burn rate (are users hurt), then symptoms (what is broken), then causes and changes (why), then one link into a single trace (prove it).

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Judging answers on documents with ANLS
md: ANLS = average over questions of the best (1 minus normalized edit distance) against any ground truth, zeroed when the distance reaches 0.5. It rewards nearly right reading, not semantic equivalence.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Privilege separation: OpenSSH's design case
md: Privilege separation protects only the code that was moved into the unprivileged half. regreSSHion (CVE-2024-6387, covered in linux-for-security) was a signal-handler race in sshd's privileged code which, in Qualys's words, "is not sandboxed and runs with full privileges". That is why OpenSSH keeps shrinking the privileged parts: the 9.8 and 10.0 splits move more code out of them.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
md: Ask legal, authorised, ethical before every task. Public data is still personal data; combining it can create a harm none of the pieces had alone.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Verifying images and claims: provenance, reposts and hashes
md: Ask where and when an image first appeared before asking whether it was edited. Perceptual hashes find reposts; provenance and corroboration decide the claim.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint
md: Understand the people-data industry so you can defend against it: brokers sell profiles, attackers use them, and you shrink exposure with settings, separation, MFA and removal requests.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CUDA builds: PTX, cubins and the architecture list
md: Cubins run only on the same major CC with an equal or higher minor; PTX JIT compiles forward to any equal or higher CC. Ship cubins for the GPUs you target plus PTX for the newest one, and keep the list short for development builds, because every entry multiplies CUDA compile time.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Flaky means uncontrolled state. Reproduce with the exact node id, order seed and loop count, find the state, and control it with a fixture. Reruns and quarantine are temporary and cost real signal.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: Whatever the tool, the author's loop is the same: answer every comment, change the code where the reviewer was right, record what changed between versions, and carry earned review credit forward only while it still applies.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Misconception: "syncing my fork" updates my laptop. GitHub's Sync fork button updates the fork on GitHub; `git fetch upstream` plus a merge updates your local copy. GitHub's docs point out that syncing locally does not update the fork on GitHub until you push. They are separate repositories.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: Misconception: `-s` signs the commit. It does not. `-s` (lowercase) adds a Signed-off-by text trailer, a legal statement. `-S` (uppercase, `--gpg-sign`) adds a cryptographic signature made with your private key, by default through GPG (GNU Privacy Guard), that GitHub can show as Verified. A project may require either, both, or neither.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: Outbound is what users get; inbound is what the project gets from you. Inbound=outbound needs no paperwork; a CLA is a one-time signed grant, often with an explicit patent license and a statement about your employer.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Reporting honestly: geomeans, many benchmarks and costs
md: Do not cherry-pick. Quoting only the best benchmark, dropping a regressed one, or rerunning until a borderline result flips are all ways to make noise look like a win. Reviewers who rerun your commands will find out.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A screenshot of a traceback is not complete. The maintainer cannot search it, copy the line numbers, or paste it into a test. Stack Overflow's guide says plainly: do not use images of code; paste text.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: The right size for a PR is **one self-contained change**: it does one thing, includes its tests, and leaves the system working. Line counts are a symptom; focus is the goal.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Why contiguous KV allocation wastes most of the memory
md: Knowing the exact output length would not fix this. Orca (Oracle) assumes perfect knowledge and still stores real token states in only 38.2% of KV memory, because contiguous chunks of different sizes still fragment the space and still cannot be shared.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: What a penetration test is, and what it is not
md: A scan asks *what might be wrong*. A pentest asks *what can an attacker actually do here, inside this scope*. A red team asks *would we notice and stop them*. A bug bounty asks the crowd, continuously, within published rules.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Attack surface management: recon as a defender
md: Attackers run recon against you continuously and for free. Run it yourself first: inventory what is exposed, diff it on a schedule, and treat every unexpected change as an incident until explained.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: Comparing two flame graphs by eye is error-prone because widths are relative to each graph's own total. To check a fix, record both under the same load and diff the folded files (a differential flame graph), and make sure you have enough samples for the change to stand out from noise.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Why people are the most attacked surface
md: Common misconception: "only careless people fall for phishing". The UK NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre) notes that people click for many reasons, including situational ones such as being busy and stressed, and that blaming them does not work. Blame also stops people reporting mistakes, which is the signal defenders need most.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Business email compromise and invoice fraud
md: BEC defeats technical email security by design: the best version comes from a real, authenticated account. The control that stops it is a payment process that does not trust email for changes to where money goes.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Layout for the cache: arrays of structs versus structs of arrays
md: Lay data out the way your hottest loop reads it: fields used together in the same line, fields read alone in their own array, rarely used fields out of the way, and data written by different threads on different lines.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Grover's algorithm, and why AES-128 is still fine
md: NIST's verdict in IR 8547: symmetric primitives with at least 128 bits of classical security meet **security category 1** (the lowest of NIST's five post-quantum levels, listed next), and NIST does not expect to transition away from them. Only the few 112-bit ones are disallowed in 2030. Spend the migration budget on RSA and elliptic curves, not on re-keying AES-128.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Deadlines and a migration plan you can defend
md: Dates differ by regulator, but the order of work does not: inventory, then key establishment on anything recorded today, then signatures, PKI and devices, all finished by 2035. The NIST dates apply at every key size; a 4096-bit RSA key is deprecated after 2030 like a 2048-bit one.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: Common misconception: "faster RAM will speed up my tree or hash-chain lookups." Faster transfer rates raise peak bandwidth, but a dependent chain of misses uses a tiny fraction of it. Its cost is set by latency, which has improved far more slowly.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Pseudonyms and hashes are not anonymity: AOL 2006
md: Pseudonyms protect the name, not the person. They link all of one person's records, and those records (queries, routes, purchases) can identify them by content. Ask what a released record says, not only what field was deleted.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy: a promise about one person
md: Differential privacy is a property of the mechanism: on any two datasets differing in one person, every output is at most e^epsilon times likelier on one than the other. It survives post-processing and any auxiliary data, and epsilons add up across releases.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Designing for less: data minimisation and purpose limitation
md: Minimise by architecture: collect less, coarsen at the edge, compute on the device, separate identity from content, enforce purposes in the access layer and in database grants, and default to the least sharing.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Rights in code: access and erasure across every copy
md: Rights are requirements on every copy: build a data map (system, lookup key, export method, erase method), meet the one-month clock (Art. 12(3)), put backups beyond use, notify recipients, and verify identity in proportion to what you would hand over.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Defending the path: segmentation, admin hygiene, EDR, HSE timeline
md: Escalation and lateral movement are a chain of small, valid-looking steps. Make each step harder (least privilege, unique and protected credentials, segmentation, patching known-exploited bugs) and make each step visible (forwarded logs, EDR, the event chains in this course), then make sure every alert has an owner.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL
md: Same scores, three uses: rerank finished solutions (weighted voting is a strong default), prune partial solutions in beam search (best on harder problems at modest budgets), or provide step-level rewards so RL can credit each step separately.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Who runs next: run queues, CFS, EEVDF and nice
md: Misconception: "nice 19 means it only runs when the machine is idle." A nice 19 task still has weight 15, so against one nice 0 task it gets about 1.4 percent. For truly leftover CPU, use the `SCHED_IDLE` policy, which the CFS document describes as even weaker than nice 19.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: IVFADC: inverted lists with residual codes
md: Raising code size cannot fix a too-small nprobe. The paper notes that increasing the code length is useless if w is not big enough, because neighbors outside the probed lists are never scored. Tune nprobe first, then code size.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Any structural comparison in this field is after optimal superposition. A reported RMSD of 1.4 Angstrom always means 1.4 after Kabsch alignment; the unaligned number is meaningless because it depends on where the coordinates happen to be written down.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Regular expressions: counting failed logins per address
md: A per-address threshold is easy to evade. Mandiant saw UNC5537 log in mostly through commercial VPN (virtual private network) addresses, and stuffing tools can spread attempts so each address fails only once or twice. Also count failures per username, and treat any success after failures as more important than the failures themselves.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Testing your script so it does not fail silently
md: Test the awkward inputs and the failure paths, not just the happy path, and keep tests offline with fakes. A test suite is what lets you change a detection script without wondering what you broke.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Interleave, step back, or fan out: IRCoT, Step-Back and multi-query
md: Pick the pattern by the question's shape: a vague or context-dependent question needs one **rewrite**; a chain of facts needs **sequential decomposition** (Self-Ask, IRCoT); an over-specific question benefits from a **step-back**; a question that could be phrased many ways benefits from **multi-query** fan-out.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Business logic flaws: when correct code does the wrong thing
md: A logic flaw is an assumption the server never checks. To find one, list what the design assumes about users (what they send, in what order, how fast, how many accounts) and ask which assumption would pay them to break.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Limit overrun: one coupon, one balance, many parallel requests
md: Claim-first works only because the Set lives in this one process. Run two Node processes, or two servers, or keep the state in a real database, and the check and the claim are separate network calls again. The durable fix puts the claim where the state is: a unique constraint or a conditional update in the database (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Hidden sub-states: Kettle's GitLab email race (CVE-2022-4037)
md: Every request is a sequence of steps, so every endpoint that edits shared state has sub-states. Decide each security-relevant value once, carry it with the work, and make the state change atomic, rather than writing a value early and reading it back later.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft safety: the election restriction and the Figure 8 trap
md: A Raft leader commits by counting replicas **only** for entries from its own current term. Older entries become committed indirectly, when a later current-term entry after them commits. Entries keep their original term number forever, which is why this rule is needed.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Query-document features: BM25 per field, coverage, proximity
md: Per-field BM25 features are not BM25F. BM25F (the subject of Elasticsearch's `combined_fields` query) merges term frequencies across fields before saturating. Separate per-field features saturate each field on its own and let the model weigh them. Both are useful; they are different numbers.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Three runs, seven verdicts: when metrics disagree
md: Disagreement between metrics is information, not noise. If binary metrics and exponential nDCG disagree, your system is trading coverage of relevant documents against putting the very best one first. Report at least one metric of each kind and say which user you care about.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Kaseya VSA and REvil, July 2021: one tool, many victims
md: Any tool that can run code on many machines (RMM, patch management, EDR consoles, software deployment) is Tier 0. Keep it off the internet, behind MFA and a dedicated admin network, and watch it as closely as a domain controller. CISA's MSP guidance adds: MSP accounts out of admin groups, a dedicated VPN for MSP traffic, and the MSP's activity logged into the customer's own monitoring.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics
md: Polling the trailer only works if the NIC writes the message in increasing address order. FaRM notes that many NICs, including theirs, guarantee this for RDMA writes but not reads. It is a hardware property, not a verbs promise: registering memory with `IBV_ACCESS_RELAXED_ORDERING` explicitly gives up write-after-write ordering.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: Interpolation is not prediction. It never invents a position: it only blends two snapshots the server really sent. The cost is that every remote entity is shown late by the buffer delay, which is why aiming needs lag compensation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
md: Space2 was shown only 23 times in 2000, although it is mobile users' second choice (0.25). Optimism-based exploration stops exploring once an arm looks clearly worse than the leader; that is the point, but it means some items get little data. Freshness boosts or explicit exploration slots are common additions.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Three ways to join two tables
md: Nested loop: cost about outer x inner-scan, works for any condition, great with an inner index and few outer rows. Merge join: one pass over each sorted input, needs sorted inputs and an equality key. Hash join: one pass over each input, needs an equality key and memory for the build side.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leaderless quorums: why R + W > N makes reads overlap writes
md: $R + W > N$ is a counting argument, nothing more: if the write really sits on W of the N designated replicas and the read really asks R of those same N, they share a replica. Lesson 4 shows how failures quietly break the "same N" part.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: KL regularization: a leash, not a cure
md: KL regularization and early stopping limit the *amount* of optimization, which keeps you on the rising side of the Goodhart curve. They cannot tell a good high-reward behavior from a bad one. Only a better reward, a conservative reward, or an outside check can do that.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
md: Governance decides who decides. Risk management decides what is worth doing. Compliance proves to outsiders that you did what you are obliged to do. They overlap, but a company can be compliant and still badly governed, or well governed and still breached.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Security economics: how much to spend (the Gordon-Loeb model)
md: Gordon-Loeb's lessons for engineers: spend where a dollar reduces the most expected loss, not where the scariest weakness is; for the paper's broad families of breach functions the optimum is at most about 37 percent of expected loss; and making controls more effective beats making budgets bigger.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: One control, many frameworks: CIS Controls, HIPAA and the crosswalk
md: Do not run one programme per framework. Write each control once, build it to the strictest applicable requirement, map it to every framework it satisfies, and attach evidence that is collected automatically. Start from CIS IG1 if you have nothing; use the crosswalk to answer everyone else.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Insurance does not replace controls or accountability. Regulators still fine you, customers still leave, and a claim can fail if your application overstated your controls or the event falls under an exclusion. Treat the policy wording as a contract engineers should read: what counts as a covered event, which notice deadlines apply, which incident responders you must use.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: After new weights land, cached KV entries are wrong: they were computed by the old weights. SGLang's `update_weights_from_distributed` flushes the cache by default, and AReaL's interruptible workers discard KV caches and recompute them with the new weights before continuing unfinished sequences.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: One fault, 397 alerts: collapsing the storm
md: Dedup and grouping are lossless: they change how many notifications you receive, not what was observed. Inhibition and silences are lossy: they delete evidence from your view. Use the first two freely and the last two sparingly.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: Do not confuse RRF's k with the k of k-nearest-neighbors. Azure AI Search's docs stress that the RRF constant is "entirely separate" from the k that sets how many neighbors a vector query returns. Elasticsearch names them `rank_constant` and `rank_window_size` to avoid the clash.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: From -ENOMEM and ERR_PTR to Result
md: `to_result` is not a general converter. For a C function that returns a byte count or an index on success, use the raw value: check `< 0` yourself or write a small wrapper that returns `Result<usize>`. Otherwise the success value silently disappears.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The baseline you replace: EEVDF picks and the knobs it offers
md: Misconception: a shorter slice buys a task more CPU. Under EEVDF it buys an earlier deadline and more, shorter turns; the total still follows the weights.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Build, load and run your own scheduler end to end
md: Misconception: the loader is just a launcher and can exit once the scheduler is attached. The link belongs to the process: when it exits, the link is destroyed and the kernel unregisters the scheduler. The loader is also the only place the exit reason gets printed.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
md: Misconception: a lower average latency means a better scheduler. A policy can cut the median and still multiply the p99, and for interactive work the tail is what users feel.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558 and a signing key that should have died in 2021
md: A signing key's real lifetime is not what the plan says but what the system enforces. Enforce expiry in code, alert on key age, and treat "we paused rotation" as a security incident with an owner and a deadline.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: JavaScript: prototype pollution and code built from strings
md: Pollution is process-wide and lasts until restart. One request can change the behaviour of every later request to that Node.js process, including other users' requests, which makes it confusing to debug and dangerous to leave running.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Heartbleed as a diff: reviewing every field of a message
md: Field checklist for any parser diff: list every value taken from outside, and for each one point to the line that validates it against a fact the code controls (the real buffer length, a maximum). An empty cell is a finding. For pointer loops, end checks use < or >=, never == or !=.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Secure channels at every layer: what each protocol protects
md: Ask two questions of any secure protocol: between which two points does the protection start and stop, and what happens to the data outside them? A VPN stops at the gateway; SSH stops at the server process; S/MIME never stops while the message stays encrypted.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Time is a security input: NTP, delay attacks and NTS
md: NTS stops forged and altered time replies; it cannot stop delay attacks, because a delayed packet is still authentic. RFC 8915 bounds the damage at MAXDIST/2 and suggests several time sources or several network paths. Combine NTS with multiple servers and alert on large clock steps.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The perimeter model, Operation Aurora and the road to BeyondCorp
md: Zero trust does not mean "no VPN" or "no firewall". BeyondCorp removed the trust that came with being on the network. Encrypted tunnels and network filters still exist in zero trust designs; they just stop being the reason anyone gets access.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Measuring the journey: CISA's maturity model and a migration plan
md: A maturity score measures capabilities, not outcomes. An agency can be Advanced in every pillar and still be breached through an unpatched edge appliance. Track both: the stage per pillar, and evidence such as how many apps still need a VPN and how many accounts still use phishable MFA.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Worked scenario: prompt injection through attacker-written log fields
md: Anything an attacker can write into a log can end up in your model's context. Give the model no authority the attacker should not have, let deterministic rules make decisions, and treat instruction-like text in a field as an indicator.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Attack surface, and the Morris worm's four doors
md: Attack surface is everything an attacker can touch: services, features, trust relationships and people. The Morris worm used all four kinds at once. The cheapest defence is removing doors you do not need (a debug command in production, an unused service); the next is making each remaining door check its input.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
md: Real attacks do not walk the phases neatly in order. Attackers loop (discover, move, discover again), skip steps (a stolen password needs no weaponization), and run phases in parallel. Use the models as a vocabulary and a checklist, not a script.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Executive summaries: one page for the person who decides
md: Do not soften the verdict to keep a client happy, and do not dramatise it to be noticed. Both destroy the summary's main asset: that the reader can take it at face value. If the news is good, say so plainly; a calibrated "the defences held" is as useful as a warning.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: A common misconception: self-play means no external signal. Games have a perfect, free judge: the rules decide who won. Take that away and a model playing against itself only amplifies its own beliefs, which is the collapse setting from the prerequisite course.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Using failures and training the judge: V-STaR, the gap, Meta-Rewarding
md: Each method buys information somewhere. V-STaR gets more out of the answer key by learning from failures; SCoRe uses the answer key to reward fixes; Meta-Rewarding has no outside signal, so it can only exploit its own generation-verification gap, which Song et al. saw shrink to about zero within a few rounds on math.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
md: Evaluate compression like a model change: measure your task metric at several ratios on your own data, and measure end-to-end latency including the compressor. The published gains were measured on specific benchmarks with specific target models.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Equifax and Spring4Shell: when the framework evaluates input
md: Equifax, Spring4Shell, ProxyLogon (lesson 14) and MOVEit all ended the same way: a **web shell** written into a directory the web server executes. Two cheap controls hit all of them: make web roots read-only to the app's own user, and alert on new script files appearing there.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
md: Prefix reuse is a property of the *whole serving path*: frontend hints, the radix tree, queue order on each worker, and routing across workers. Each layer can preserve reuse or destroy it.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
md: Production routing = a graph from OSM (directed, with turn costs) + a preprocessing technique. CH gives the fastest queries on a fixed metric; partition-based MLD or CRP accepts new weights in seconds without redoing the expensive phase.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
md: Two ceilings limit SIMD: latency chains (fix with several independent accumulators) and memory bandwidth (fix by doing more work per byte or keeping data in cache). Lane count only matters once both are out of the way.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
md: Bump allocation costs a few instructions and has no per-object free. It is ideal when a group of objects share one lifetime (a request, a frame, a compiler pass) and wrong when objects die at unrelated times, because one long-lived object keeps the whole arena alive.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
md: A resumed partial sample can contain tokens generated by several weight versions. `--mask-offpolicy-in-partial-rollout` removes the old prefix tokens from the loss, but the docs note this does not remove the prefix-distribution mismatch: the newer tokens that are trained were still generated after a prefix the current policy might not have written.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Suspicious logins: impossible travel and MFA push spam
md: The CSRB's review of the group known as Lapsus$ found that, in a few cases, the attackers "impersonated help desk personnel over direct chat messages and encouraged employees to approve the MFA prompts". When you contact a user about an alert, use a channel the attacker cannot be sitting in, and teach users that the real SOC never asks them to approve a prompt.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Metrics, burnout and the analyst's ethics
md: The analyst's job, in one sentence: answer each alert with evidence, quickly and in order of risk, write it down so others can act and check, and use the access that makes this possible only for that purpose.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: SIM swaps, bribed insiders and people you do not employ
md: People outside your organisation (carrier staff, outsourced agents, contractors) can be the weak link for your accounts. Design so that no single outside person's mistake or bribe hands over a login, and make reporting approaches normal inside.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
md: Words to keep apart: a **latent** is a unit of the SAE; a **feature** is the concept you hope it captures. Gemma Scope says 'latents' for exactly this reason. A latent with a clean name is a hypothesis about a model feature, not proof of one. Lesson 5 shows how a latent gets its name and how that name is tested.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
md: High variance explained is not full understanding. Sonnet's SAEs explained at least 65% of variance, so a sizeable part of the activation lives in the error term, and a latent's top activating examples do not prove what it does. Use ablation or steering to check.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
md: The variogram turns Tobler's law into numbers: how much readings disagree, on average, as a function of distance. Its nugget, sill and range are what kriging uses to decide weights.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
md: Speculative sampling is exact in math, not bit for bit. Chen et al. note samples match the target 'within hardware numerics': different batching, kernels and random number streams change floating point results, so a fixed seed will not reproduce plain decoding token for token.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: CTC and wav2vec 2.0: training without frame-level alignments
md: Two families: CTC models (like wav2vec 2.0 fine-tuned) classify every frame and collapse the path, so output is tied to audio frames. Encoder-decoder models (like Whisper) generate text with a decoder that also acts as a language model, which buys punctuation and multitask prompts and brings language-model failure modes such as loops.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
md: `free` rarely shrinks your process. Freed small chunks go back on glibc's free lists, not to the kernel, and a single live chunk near the top of the heap blocks trimming. A process whose memory never drops after a burst is usually not leaking; check whether the memory is reusable before hunting leaks.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
md: A non-NULL return from `malloc` does not mean the memory exists. Under default overcommit a large allocation succeeds immediately, and the failure, if any, comes later as an OOM kill when the pages are first written, far from the line that allocated them.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Lab: build, sweep and evaluate a steering vector on a small chat model
md: Report a steering vector with: the model, layer, positions and coefficient; build, validation and test splits and their sizes; the behavior score on test across coefficients; a random vector of equal norm; a prompting baseline; KL or loss on unrelated prompts plus a capability score; generations you actually read; and the per-input spread (lesson 7).

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Online filtering: EMA as a low-pass, Welford for anomaly flags
md: Online operators keep O(1) state per key and update per reading. Mean and variance via Welford are order-independent; the EMA is not. Both are cheap enough to run per sensor in the stream processor.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Multi-head attention by hand: two heads, two patterns
md: Head A only *looks* like a previous-token head. It matches content: these four words happen to be distinct and in this order. Shuffle the sentence and it follows the words, not the positions. A real positional head needs the position information that Lesson 5 adds.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
md: Attention trades sequential steps for quadratic pairwise work. That is a great deal on GPUs for moderate n, and the reason long-context methods all target the n x n score matrix.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
md: `block_size` is the **maximum** context, not the only context. Because position $t$ in each chunk sees only $t+1$ tokens, the model is trained on every context length from 1 to `block_size`, which is exactly what it needs when generation starts from a short prompt.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
md: Training scores all positions in parallel with teacher forcing; generation is a sequential loop over the same network that samples from the last position's distribution, shaped by temperature, top-k or top-p.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
md: Steepest descent is a local statement. $-\nabla f(2, 1) = (-4, -6)$ does not point at the minimum $(0, 0)$, which lies in direction $(-2, -1)$. In an elongated bowl the gradient mostly points across the narrow valley, which is why plain gradient descent (repeatedly stepping against the gradient, lesson 6) zig-zags.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Files, paths and permissions: finding your way around
md: `rm` and `mv` act at once and say nothing. `mv` onto an existing name silently replaces that file, and `rm -r` cannot be undone. Before deleting with a pattern, run `ls` with the same pattern to see what it matches, and add `-i` to make `rm` or `mv` ask first.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Pipes: concurrent processes, sort | uniq -c, and SIGPIPE
md: A pipeline is several processes running concurrently and connected by bounded kernel buffers. Fast writers block on a full pipe; writers to a closed pipe get SIGPIPE. Tools like `sort` that need all their input are where a pipeline stops streaming.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux
md: The private key works like your password on every server that lists its public key. Never copy it to a server or commit it to a repository, and protect it with a passphrase; `ssh-agent` can hold the unlocked key so you type the passphrase once per session.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Embeddings for IDs: categorical features, hashing and weight tying
md: An ID embedding is trained by whatever loss it feeds. Supervised losses place IDs with similar effects on the target close together. When the ID space is huge or open, trade exactness for a fixed-size table: hash, share an unknown row, or build vectors from features.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
md: Reserving the maximum length for every request wastes most of the cache. vLLM's profiling found only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV memory held actual token states in earlier systems, due to reserved slots and fragmentation. PagedAttention fixes this by allocating the cache in small fixed-size blocks, like OS pages.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
md: Control flow is the program counter. Straight-line code advances it by the instruction length; `jmp`, conditional jumps, `call` and `ret` overwrite it. A C `for` loop compiles to a compare plus a conditional jump backwards.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why real CPUs beat the simple loop: pipelines and prediction
md: Pipelining raises throughput, not the speed of any single instruction. The flow breaks on dependencies on recent results and on jumps the predictor gets wrong; a misprediction costs roughly the pipeline's length in cycles.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
md: SFT does not add much new knowledge. If the base model does not know a fact, a demonstration that states it mostly teaches the model to answer confidently in that style, which can increase made-up answers on other questions ([Gekhman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05904)).

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
md: An inverted index maps each term to a sorted list of the documents that contain it. A query reads only the postings of its own terms, so the work depends on how common those terms are, not on how big the whole collection is.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
md: Production inverted indexes are sorted, gap-encoded and block-compressed, and are written once into immutable segments that get merged, not edited in place. The ranking formula on top is a replaceable component.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
md: A null pointer or an uninitialized pointer does not point to any object, and dereferencing it is *undefined behavior*: the C standard places no requirements on what happens. Often you get a crash (a segmentation fault on Linux: the process touched an address with no memory mapped there, so the operating system kills it), but the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, so do not rely on a crash to tell you.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Structs and linked data: ->, typedef and a linked list
md: Never touch a node after freeing it, and that includes reading its next field to continue a loop. Save every pointer you still need from a block before you free the block.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Debugging C: gdb and Valgrind on a real crash
md: On the Mac used for this course, the ASan runtime in Apple's clang refused leak detection: running with `ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1` printed `detect_leaks is not supported on this platform`. On Linux, ASan's leak check is on by default. Check leaks where your tools support them, for example in Linux CI.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: The rule is not "only one reference to a variable per function". Sequential borrows are fine, as are many shared ones. The error only appears when a `&mut` borrow overlaps any other live borrow of the same value.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Closures and threads: moving ownership to another thread
md: A thread gets values by ownership: `move` them into its closure, `send` them through a channel, get them back from `join`. Since every value has one owner, two threads cannot both reach it unless a type built for sharing is in between.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
md: `A * B` in NumPy and PyTorch is the **element-wise** (Hadamard, after the mathematician Jacques Hadamard) product, which multiplies entries in matching positions, not matrix multiplication. Matrix multiplication is `A @ B` (or `np.matmul`). With two same-shape square matrices both run without error and give different answers, so this bug is silent.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Tensors, batches and broadcasting: shapes in real code
md: Tensors are arrays with any number of axes; `@` multiplies the last two and broadcasts the rest. Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right, and sizes must be equal or 1. Name the axis a reduction removes, and keep it with `keepdims=True` when you broadcast back.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Mini-batches: noisy gradients and the training loop
md: SGD steps on an unbiased but noisy gradient estimate from a minibatch. Noise falls only as $1/\sqrt B$, so moderate batches with many steps are usually the efficient choice.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Early stopping and why big models still generalize
md: Gradient descent fits high-curvature, smooth directions first and nearly flat, wiggly ones last. Noise lives mostly in the flat directions, so stopping at the best validation error keeps the signal and skips the noise. That is why early stopping acts like an L2 penalty.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: What hidden units compute: hinges, cuts and new features
md: A ReLU hidden unit is a hinge (one input) or a cut with a ramp (many inputs). The output layer adds these up into a piecewise-linear function, and equivalently, it runs a linear model on the features the hidden layer computed.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Build it: a tiny autograd engine from scratch
md: Gradients accumulate across calls too. In this engine, `backward()` resets only the output's grad, so calling it twice on `f = x * x` with `x = 3` leaves `x.grad` at 12, not 6. That is why part 3 zeroes every parameter's grad before each backward pass, and why PyTorch training loops call `opt.zero_grad()`.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
md: A page fault is not a bug. It is a legal access to a page that happens not to be in memory, and the program never notices except as a delay. A segmentation fault is different: an access to an invalid page, which the OS treats as an error.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Files and directories: the API and how vsfs finds your data
md: Directories map names to inode numbers; inodes map file offsets to disk blocks; the per-process descriptor and the open file table remember where you are. Path lookup costs disk reads in proportion to the path's depth unless the cache has the blocks.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
md: The classic mistake is confusing $P(E \mid H)$ with $P(H \mid E)$, called base rate neglect. It shows up in ML with a classifier on a rare class. Its **recall** is $P(\text{flagged} \mid \text{positive class})$, the sensitivity, and does not depend on the base rate; its **precision** is $P(\text{positive class} \mid \text{flagged})$, the posterior, and does. High recall can still come with mostly false alarms.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
md: One matrix, Sigma, holds every pairwise covariance. Any weighted sum has variance a-transpose Sigma a, and a Gaussian with covariance Sigma is just mu + L z with independent standard normals z.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it
md: Before launching, choose alpha, power and the minimum effect worth detecting, then compute n. Do not stop early on a peek unless the method allows it, and report the effect with its interval.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Kaplan vs Chinchilla: why 2020-era models were undertrained
md: Misconception: Kaplan's power laws were wrong. The loss-versus-size and loss-versus-data trends were real and still hold in shape. What shifted was the **compute-optimal allocation** derived from them, which is sensitive to experimental details. A scaling law is only as good as the runs it was fitted on.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, online tests
md: By default trec_eval silently ignores queries for which a run retrieved nothing, so a system that crashes on hard queries can score higher. Pass -c to average over every query in the qrels, with missing queries scored 0.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
md: Misconception: a higher similarity score means a more relevant passage across queries. Cosine scores are only comparable within one query's ranking and one model. A fixed threshold like 0.7 that works for one model can be meaningless for another.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Build a byte-level BPE tokenizer in Python
md: A byte-level BPE tokenizer is three small functions: train (count pairs, merge the top one, mint ids from 256), encode (apply merges by lowest id) and decode (join bytes, decode UTF-8 with errors replaced). The regex split adds one rule: count and merge inside chunks only.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Optimizers: momentum, Adam and decoupled weight decay
md: Adam's step is about **lr in size regardless of gradient scale**. That is its strength, and also why L2 regularization inside Adam misbehaves. Use AdamW when you want weight decay with an adaptive optimizer.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
md: Cosine similarity and inner product are not the same metric. If your embeddings are not unit-length, an inner-product index ranks differently from cosine. Faiss (Meta's open-source vector search library) documents the standard fix: normalize vectors to length 1. Cosine is the inner product divided by both lengths, so when both lengths are 1 the two are equal.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Install scripts: why installing a package runs its code
md: Blocking install scripts stops code that runs at install time. It does not stop malicious code that runs when your app imports the package, or a `.pth` file that Python runs on start-up. It removes the easiest path, not every path.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: When a dependency is compromised: a response playbook
md: Malicious dependency equals intrusion. Scope by version and time window, contain, assume every machine that ran it is compromised, rotate secrets from a clean machine, hunt, rebuild, then fix the control that failed.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Verification is the fix: why filtered self-training does not collapse
md: The generator does not have to be right; the kept set has to be. Collapse is avoided when a verifier keeps more correct than incorrect examples, and its judgments must track this generator's actual errors.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
md: `mmap` signals failure with `MAP_FAILED`, which is `(void *) -1`, not `NULL`. Code that checks `if (p == NULL)` misses every error and later dereferences address -1.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
md: `MAP_FIXED` forcibly replaces whatever is already mapped at that address. In a multithreaded program another thread (or a library calling `dlopen`, which loads a shared library at run time, or `malloc`) may have just mapped something there, and you silently destroy it. mmap(2) recommends `MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE`, which fails with `EEXIST` (already exists) instead of clobbering.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
md: *Present* and a missing end date are not the same thing. *Present* is an explicit claim of a current role. A blank end date may mean the person forgot to fill it in. Pick a convention, store which case occurred, and do not silently treat blanks as current.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau
md: Repeated sampling scales **coverage** smoothly; selection without a reliable checker does not keep up. The useful question is never only how many samples, but how good is the verifier at the tail.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Sequential thinking lets later tokens build on earlier ones, which parallel sampling cannot. s1 found that majority voting over the base model could not catch up with the budget-forced fine-tuned model.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
md: Every number here is one group's runs at 760M parameters or less. A later public reimplementation (lesson 8) found the full model did not always beat its baselines, while the memory itself consistently helped over attention-only variants.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
md: Every modern malloc fast path is the same idea as the 2001 magazine layer: a small, private stack of free objects per thread or CPU, refilled and drained in batches from a locked shared layer, with sizing policies to cap the memory that sits idle.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Measuring a hunt programme, and where to practise
md: Measure a hunt programme by what it changes: detections created, gaps and vulnerabilities closed, techniques examined, and the dwell time of anything it finds. Intrusions found matter most when they happen, but a quarter without one is not a failed quarter if the organisation is harder to attack at the end of it.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Kill chain and ATT&CK as analytic frames
md: Use the kill chain to ask "where can we act against this adversary, and how many independent ways?" and ATT&CK to ask "which of their known behaviours can we see?". Both answer defender decisions, which is why they belong in intelligence products.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack surface: every door, window and vent
md: "Internal only" is not off the surface. An endpoint reachable only from inside the network is still reachable by anyone who gets inside: a phished employee, a compromised vendor login, a malicious insider. Count it, and protect it as if the network were hostile.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
md: Third-party access is a trust boundary you do not fully control. Give each vendor the narrowest path, watch it closely, and assume the vendor's own computers may already be compromised.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A forecast is a prediction made at an origin $T$ using only data up to $T$, for a stated horizon $h$. Every evaluation in this course respects that constraint.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Reading an X.509 certificate field by field
md: Common misconception: "the CN must match the hostname". Modern clients ignore CN for name matching and check SAN only; a certificate with the right CN but no matching SAN entry fails in browsers and in Python's ssl module.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Your first kernel: program_id, offsets and masks
md: `tl.load` with a mask but no `other=` leaves masked lanes **undefined**. That is safe only if those lanes never feed a result. Any reduction (sum, max) over a masked block needs `other=` set to the operation's neutral value: the value that leaves the result unchanged, 0 for a sum (x + 0 = x) and minus infinity for a max (max(x, -inf) = x).

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Continuous images: one transformer, two losses
md: Misconception: "lambda is just a weight, any value works." Text cross-entropy and noise MSE live on different scales, and lambda decides how the shared weights split their capacity. Transfusion used 5, BAGEL effectively 4 (0.25 CE + 1 MSE is a quarter of CE + 4 MSE). Change the noise parameterization or schedule and the right value moves.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code
md: Build-time specialization = **pick components by configuration, link statically, let DCE and LTO remove the rest**. Reconfiguring means rebuilding.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
md: At hundreds of dimensions, a distance does about 0.5 to 0.75 FLOPs per byte of vector it reads. SIMD makes the arithmetic cheap; after that, the bytes you move (and the cache misses you take) decide the speed.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
md: Turning on mmap does not shrink an index; it only lets the OS evict parts of it. If the hot working set does not fit, latency can fall off a cliff, because each miss is a disk read instead of a DRAM access.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Why an hour of video does not fit: frames times tokens
md: Video cost is **frames x tokens per frame**. Every long-video method attacks one factor: fewer frames (sampling), fewer tokens per frame (pooling), fewer tokens over time (merging, memory), a bigger budget (long context), or a different representation (text captions).

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Where ViT-B/16's 86 million parameters live
md: A ViT-B/16 backbone is 85.8M parameters, 99% of them in 12 identical blocks of 7.09M each, and two thirds of each block is MLP. The classification head is tiny: 77,669 parameters for 101 classes.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: From a VLM that describes to a VLA that acts
md: Misconception: web pretraining teaches the robot new motions. It does not. Web knowledge helps decide *which* object and *where*; the motor skills themselves still come from robot demonstrations.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: FSQ and LFQ: quantizers with no learned codebook
md: FSQ and LFQ trade a learned codebook for a fixed grid. You lose the freedom to place codes where the data is dense, and gain full usage by construction, no codebook loss, and vocabularies of 2^16 to 2^18 that VQ struggles to use.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: CUDA graphs: padding, support levels and mode downgrades
md: CUDA graphs constrain attention through shape (pad to a captured size), address (persistent metadata buffers) and kernel choice (`AttentionCGSupport`). The weakest backend in the model sets the graph mode for everyone.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Where VLMs fail and how they are evaluated
md: A high benchmark score does not mean the model looked at the image. The BlindTest paper cites prior work finding that 42.9% of MMMU questions can be answered without the image. Build a small eval from your own documents, with the image-free baseline as a control.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Making wait-free fast: fast path, slow path, and when to bother
md: Check every layer. A wait-free algorithm is only as wait-free as its primitives and helpers: a `fetch_or` that compiles to a CAS loop, an allocator that takes a lock, or a reclamation scheme that can block will each reintroduce unbounded waiting.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Web testing as work: pentests, disclosure programmes and bounties
md: A pentest buys coverage of an agreed scope; a bug bounty buys the first valid report of each root cause; a VDP buys reports without payment. In all three the written rules, published or signed before testing, are what make the work legal.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: File inclusion: when a path parameter chooses the code that runs
md: Path traversal reads a file; file inclusion runs it. The fix for both is the same idea: the user picks from a list the server owns, never a path.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Origins and sites: how the browser names who owns a page
md: Same-site is not same-origin. `login.example.com` and `blog.example.com` are same-site but cross-origin. A weak subdomain (an old blog, a marketing page run by a vendor) is "same-site" with your login page, and cookie rules and SameSite (lesson 5) treat it as a friend.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Site isolation: separate processes as a second wall
md: Site isolation is **defence in depth** for the browser itself. It does not change what web pages are allowed to do, so it will not stop XSS, CSRF or a bad CORS policy. It limits the damage when the browser's own enforcement fails.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: SMB file shares and EternalBlue: how WannaCry spread
md: Worms need two things: a reachable service and a bug in it. Patching removes the bug; turning off SMBv1 and blocking 445 removes the reachability. Do both, because you will never patch everything on time.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Public Wi-Fi and captive portals in the HTTPS era
md: On public Wi-Fi, TLS with correct certificate validation is what protects you, not the Wi-Fi layer. The risks that remain are the places where TLS is missing (first HTTP request, portal page) or broken (apps that skip validation).

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
md: Misconception: more workers always means more throughput. With one locked queue, past the knee extra workers only add waiters on the same lock and the same cache line. The model here is deliberately simple, but the cap of 1/c is real for any serial section.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes
md: WSD is **not fully schedule-free**. Optimal peak LR still shifts with training length: Bergsma et al. (2025) quote Shen et al. puzzling that the best WSD LRs differ by token count, and Hägele et al. found the best cooldown peak LR was about half the best cosine peak. Tune the peak LR at roughly the length you care about; lesson 7 gives the evidence and a rule for adjusting it.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: MSG_ZEROCOPY: sending from your own memory safely
md: Writing into a buffer before its id completes does not crash anything, but it corrupts your own stream: the modified bytes may go out on the wire or in a retransmission. The kernel docs: kernel integrity is not affected, but a buggy program can corrupt its own data stream.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Evaluating zero-shot classifiers and choosing thresholds
md: Zero-shot replaces training data with design choices. Make those choices on a labeled dev set: compare templates or descriptions, pick argmax or per-label thresholds by the cost of errors, and re-check whenever the labels change.
